subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the circle passing through (4,1), (6,5) and having the centre on the line 4x + 3y − 24 = 0.

mark_split.label: Use the line the centre lies on

insider_note: Only two points are given, so one distance equation is all the circle offers — the line the centre lies on is the second equation, and it is used exactly as printed, not rearranged.

steps.label: Equation from SA = SB
steps.margin_note: Two marks. With only two points there is one distance equation, so it carries more weight than in a three-point question.
steps.memory_tip: Two points give one equation. The line given in the question is the second.
lines: Let S(x₁, y₁) be the centre of the circle.
S is the same distance from A and B.
steps.why: Two points fix only the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, not a single centre. The centre lies somewhere on that bisector, which is what equation (1) says.
common_mistakes: Expecting a third point and stopping when none is given.
Collecting 16 + 1 = 17 and 36 + 25 = 61 but subtracting in the wrong direction.

steps.label: Use the line the centre lies on
steps.margin_note: One mark. Write the given line with x₁ and y₁ in it — the centre is the point that has to satisfy it.
steps.memory_tip: The centre lies on the line, so its coordinates satisfy the line’s equation.
steps.why: Saying a point lies on a line means its coordinates make the line equation true. That turns the geometric condition into the second algebraic equation.
common_mistakes: Substituting one of the given points into the line instead of the centre.
Changing the line to 4x + 3y = 24 and then dropping the sign later.

steps.label: Solve for the centre
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both equations have 4x₁, so subtracting removes x₁ immediately.
steps.memory_tip: Both equations start with 4x₁. Subtract and only y₁ is left.
steps.why: The centre is where the perpendicular bisector of AB meets the given line. Both equations already carry 4x₁, so one subtraction is enough.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the other way round and getting y₁ = −4.

steps.label: Find the radius
steps.margin_note: One mark. r² = 10 is not a perfect square, so keep it as 10 and never take the root.
steps.memory_tip: Check with the other point as well: (3 − 6)² + (4 − 5)² = 9 + 1 = 10 too.
lines: A = (4, 1) lies on the circle, so r = SA.
steps.why: Either given point serves. Computing r² from B as well is a further check: (3 − 6)² + (4 − 5)² = 10, the same value, which confirms the centre.
common_mistakes: Measuring from the origin instead of from a given point.

steps.label: Equation of the circle
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Constant term: 9 + 16 − 10 = 15.
lines: Circle with centre (3, 4) and r² = 10 is
steps.why: Expanding gives the general form with g = −3, f = −4 and c = 15. A quick check is that g² + f² − c = 9 + 16 − 15 = 10 = r², as it must be.
common_mistakes: Getting the constant as 25 by forgetting to subtract r².
Leaving the answer in the centre-radius form.
